output.title: Rollback plans are not the real control
output.body:
Rollback plans sound tidy until you look at the workflow itself. In a small business, the real risk is usually not whether you can undo something later. It is what happens while the automation is already moving data, replies, or records forward.

If the wrong customer answer goes out, a duplicate invoice is created, or a manual check gets skipped, rollback only returns you to the old state after the damage has started. It does not stop the mistake from spreading. For an owner, the better question is simpler: what gate stops this from being committed in the first place?

That is the bounded decision to make before you automate anything. Pick one repeatable workflow you are considering, then name the three failure modes that would hurt most: wrong data, missed items, and duplicates. After that, choose one human approval step that blocks the worst case before it reaches payment, the inbox, or the CRM. If you are testing invoice extraction, for example, you can spot-check a small batch against the source documents before anything is posted. That is a control. Rollback is still useful, but it is the backup plan, not the main defense.

Bareni’s policy is that accounts and tools stay in the customer’s name and finished code is handed over, but that is no-lock-in positioning, not a warranty. The practical next step is still the same: decide the control first, then decide whether the automation belongs there at all.
